'''John David Reppy''' (born February 16, 1931) is a [[physicist]] and the John L. Wetherill Professor of Physics Emeritus at [[Cornell University]].  He studies the quantum properties of [[superfluid]]s such as [[helium]]. His experiments demonstrated the first evidence of topological phase transitions in superfluids.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Physicist John Reppy wins Buckley Prize {{!}} Department of Physics|url=https://physics.cornell.edu/news/physicist-john-reppy-wins-buckley-prize|website=physics.cornell.edu|date=2025-11-11|access-date=2025-12-02|language=en}}</ref>

Reppy is also a notable [[rock climber]] of long standing. He established a number of widely known climbing routes particularly in the northeastern United States.

==Early life and education==
John David Reppy was born February 16, 1931, in [[Lakehurst, New Jersey]]. His father was stationed at the [[Lakehurst Maxfield Field|US Naval Air Station]], where he worked with helium as a [[lifting gas]] for naval [[Aerostat|lighter-than-air aviation]]. The family moved almost every year to follow his military placements, including an assignment to [[Pearl Harbor]] prior to [[World War II]]. In 1943 he was sent to the western Pacific and the rest of the family settled in [[Haddam Neck]], [[Connecticut]].   

In Connecticut John Reppy became interested in [[herpetology]], [[geology]] and [[rock climbing]], exploring local quarries. He graduated from high school in 1950.<ref name="Reppy">{{cite journal |last1=Reppy |first1=John D. |title=Reflections on 65 Years of Helium Research |journal=Annual Review of Condensed Matter Physics |date=10 March 2022 |volume=13 |issue=1 |pages=1–12 |doi=10.1146/annurev-conmatphys-031620-105045 |bibcode=2022ARCMP..13....1R |s2cid=247388597 |url=https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-conmatphys-031620-105045 |access-date=21 March 2022 |issn=1947-5454|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Reppy immediately enrolled at the [[University of Connecticut]], beginning with summer school. He majored in mathematics but also began working for his thermodynamics instructor Charles Reynolds. At this time Reppy became friends with [[David M. Lee]], who was also a student. Reppy received a bachelor's degree in math and physics in 1954 at University of Connecticut and a master's degree from the same school two years later.<ref name="Lecture"/>

In 1956, Reppy joined Cecil T. Lane's Yale Low Temperature group at [[Yale University]].  As part of his Ph.D. work, Reppy adapted a design by [[Jesse Beams]] and built an apparatus for rotating a container of liquid helium in vacuum and measuring the helium's angular momentum.  He completed his dissertation in 1960,<ref name="Reppy"/> and received his PhD from Yale University in 1961.<ref name="AIP">{{cite web |title=Reppy, John David |url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11608026.html |website=American Institute of Physics |access-date=21 March 2022}}</ref>  Reppy spent 1961  working with [[Nicholas Kurti]] in [[Oxford]] on a [[National Science Foundation]] (NSF) Fellowship.<ref name="Reppy"/>

==Rock climbing==
In the 1950s and 60s, Reppy was active on [[Ragged Mountain (Connecticut)|Ragged Mountain]] in [[Connecticut]] where he collaborated on many first ascents and on publishing an area guidebook with Sam Streibert. The well-known Reppy's Crack on [[Cannon Mountain (New Hampshire)|Cannon Mountain]] in New Hampshire bears his name and he has made first ascents as of  number of routes in the [[Shawangunks]] and elsewhere. He made early attempts on Armadillo, a long alpine rock climb on [[Mount Katahdin]], [[Maine]]. In addition, he has climbed extensively in England, the [[Alps]] and western America.

Reppy has said his earliest interest in rock climbing as a very young teenager was related to the re-opening of small open-pit mica mines in eastern Connecticut during World War II in response to increased war-time demand for electronics materials.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://raggedmtn.org/ctclimbingoverview.html| title=Climbing in Connecticut| publisher=Ragged Mountain Foundation| url-status=dead| archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20081201125219/http://www.raggedmtn.org/ctclimbingoverview.html| archivedate=2008-12-01}}</ref><ref>{{cite web| url=http://mcis.western.edu/~jpeterson/me/ragged/index.html| title=The 1964 Climbing Guide to Ragged Mountain| publisher=MCIS.western.edu| url-status=dead| archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20081121153949/http://mcis.western.edu/~jpeterson/me/ragged/index.html| archivedate=2008-11-21}}</ref>

Reppy was among the first climbers in the United States to practice so-called "[[clean climbing]]" techniques, which he learned in England. While most climbers of the day were hammering their way up the cliffs with pitons, Reppy helped introduce the use of nuts, which at the time consisted of hex nuts from truck wheels, strung with nylon webbing. Unlike pitons, nuts are placed and removed without the use of hammers and save the rock from permanent damage. The technique often makes placements easier and faster to achieve, and thus may make difficult climbs easier to complete. Many advances in rock climbing were made possible by this method. Among a substantial number of others deserving credit for this trend in the U.S. are [[Yvon Chouinard]] and [[John Stannard]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.outdoors.org/publications/outdoors/2007/classic-northeast-climbs3.cfm|title=Classic Northeast Climbs | publisher=Appalachian Mountain Club}}</ref>

==Scientific career==
Reppy returned to [[New Haven, Connecticut]], in 1962, and spent four years as an assistant professor at Yale University. He joined the [[Cornell University]] Physics Department in 1966, becoming the John Wetherill Professor of Physics in 1987.<ref name="AIP"/>
As physics professor at Cornell University, he studies quantum properties of superfluids with an emphasis on boundary conditions and phase transitions in systems of reduced dimensionality. 

In 1978, Reppy and David J. Bishop measured the moment of inertia of a helium-coated mylar sheet, studying the phase transitions.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Study of the Superfluid Transition in Two-Dimensional He 4 Films|url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.40.1727|journal=Physical Review Letters|date=1978-06-26|issn=0031-9007|pages=1727–1730|volume=40|issue=26|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.40.1727|language=en|first=D. J.|last=Bishop|first2=J. D.|last2=Reppy|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> They found important differences between laminar superfluidity compared to the bulk behaviour.<ref name=":0" /> [[David Robert Nelson]] and [[J. Michael Kosterlitz]] studied the connection between the [[Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless transition]] and the experiments of Reppy and Bishop, identifying a [[topological order]].<ref name=":0" />

Physicists generally agree that the atoms in [[superfluid]] [[helium-4]] is not a Bose–Einstein condensate in the original sense of the term because its atoms interact too strongly. Reppy studied an exception: tiny amounts of helium trapped in nanometer-sized pores of a spongelike glass called [[Vycor]]. Even though the pores keep its atoms too far apart to jostle one another much, the helium still behaves like a three-dimensional fluid. In 1983 Reppy and colleagues reported results that suggested the helium was sloshing through the glass as a true Bose–Einstein condensate.<ref name=":1" /> 

Reppy's research group has close associations with [[David M. Lee]] and [[Robert Coleman Richardson|Robert C. Richardson]] also of Cornell, who shared the 1996 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] with [[Douglas D. Osheroff]] for discoveries related to super fluidity in [[helium-3]] ice. Lee, in his Nobel Prize speech, credited Reppy's "extraordinary technical ingenuity"  in experiments leading to the discovery. In the speech, Lee made other references to Reppy, noting that his work helped confirm related insights.<ref>{{cite journal| first = David M.| last =  Lee | title = The Extraordinary Phases of Liquid Helium | publisher = Nobel Prize website | date = 1996-12-07 | url = http://nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/1996/lee-lecture.pdf | accessdate = 2009-01-06}}</ref>

Reppy's work form 1983 also figured at least on the fringes of the 2001 Nobel Prize for Physics which was awarded to [[Eric Cornell]] and [[Carl Wieman]] of the [[JILA]], in Boulder, Colo., and [[Wolfgang Ketterle]] of the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]. [[Bose–Einstein condensation]] was predicted in 1924, and was seen decades ago in liquid helium, according to Ketterle, who acknowledged a controversial earlier claim by Reppy. Ketterle says that Reppy brought this finding to his attention, and that the priority claim was fair. "I think the results appeared conclusive", Ketterle reportedly said.  Co-laureate Wieman reportedly said that Reppy's claim is "really a stretch" and that "Ketterle is being gracious".<ref name=":1">{{cite web |url=http://bric.postech.ac.kr/science/97now/02_2now/020222c.html|title=New State of Matter Not So New?|publisher=Science Now|date=22 February 2002|accessdate=2009-01-06|last=Cho|first=Adrian|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110927050622/http://bric.postech.ac.kr/science/97now/02_2now/020222c.html|archive-date=27 September 2011}}</ref>

Separately, work from Cornell physics laboratories has been used to test a theory of [[cosmic strings]], hypothetical objects, which may have been important in the formation of galaxies, and may have arisen through  "phase transitions" in a fraction of a second after the [[Big Bang]].<ref>{{cite press release | url=http://nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/1996/press.html| publisher=Nobel Prize Website |title= A breakthrough in low-temperature physics|date=1996-10-09|accessdate=2009-01-06}}</ref>

==Awards==
Reppy is the recipient of numerous awards and honors, including the [[Fritz London]] Memorial Prize in 1981 and the NASA Distinguished Public Service Medal for leadership and support to the [[NASA]] microgravity fundamental physics program in 2000. Reppy is also a member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] (1988).<ref name="Lecture">{{cite web | url=http://www.phys.uconn.edu/PDF/news_01_08.pdf | publisher=Physics Department of University of Connecticut|title=2004 Charles A. Reynolds Distinguished Lecture in Physics|date=July 2004 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=http://funphysics.jpl.nasa.gov/technical/library/sig-events-00/sig000505-science-c.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010306130201/http://funphysics.jpl.nasa.gov/technical/library/sig-events-00/sig000505-science-c.html | url-status=dead | archive-date=2001-03-06 | publisher=NASA | title=Prof. John Reppy to Receive NASA Medal|date=2000-05-05 }}</ref> In 2025, the 2026 [[Oliver E. Buckley Prize]] was awarded to Reppy, David J. Bishop, Gwendal Fève and [[Michael James Manfra]] for "groundbreaking experiments that uncovered the role of vortices in the superfluid phase transition in helium films and observed anyonic braiding statistics of quasiparticles in the fractional quantum Hall effect, thus establishing the significance of topological excitations in two-dimensions."<ref name=":0" />
